prompt:
Given positive integers $n$ and $k$, say that $n$ is *$k$-solvable* if there are positive integers $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k$ (not necessarily distinct) such that
$$\frac1{a_1}+\frac1{a_2}+\dots+\frac1{a_k}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad a_1+a_2+\dots+a_k=n.$$
Prove that if $n$ is $k$-solvable, then $42n+12$ is $(k+3)$-solvable.
answer: Take $42a_1,\dots,42a_k,2,3,7$: reciprocals sum to $\frac1{42}+\frac12+\frac13+\frac17=1$ and the sum is $42n+12$.

solutions.title: Explicit construction
solutions.body:
Let $a_1,\dots,a_k$ witness that $n$ is $k$-solvable. Define $b_i=42a_i$ for $1\le i\le k$ and $b_{k+1}=2$, $b_{k+2}=3$, $b_{k+3}=7$. Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k+3}\frac1{b_i}=\frac1{42}\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{a_i}+\frac12+\frac13+\frac17=\frac1{42}+\frac{21+14+6}{42}=\frac{1}{42}+\frac{41}{42}=1,$$
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k+3}b_i=42\sum_{i=1}^ka_i+2+3+7=42n+12.$$
So $42n+12$ is $(k+3)$-solvable. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist polynomials $P$ and $Q$ with real coefficients such that for every real number $x$, we have $P(x)\ge0$, $Q(x)\ge0$, and
$$1-x^n=(1-x)P(x)+(1+x)Q(x).$$

solutions.title: Two cases
solutions.body:
**$n$ odd.** Let $P(x)=1+x+\dots+x^{n-1}$ and $Q=0$. Then $(1-x)P(x)=1-x^n$. $P\ge0$ everywhere: if $x\ge0$ all terms are nonnegative; if $x<0$ then $1-x>0$ and, as $n$ is odd, $x^n<0<1$, so $P(x)=\frac{1-x^n}{1-x}>0$.

**$n$ even.** Let $R(x)=\frac12\sum_{k=0}^{n/2-1}x^{2k}$, a sum of even powers with positive coefficients, so $R(x)\ge0$ for all real $x$. By the geometric series, $2(1-x^2)R(x)=(1-x^2)\sum_{k<n/2}x^{2k}=1-x^n$. Put
$$P(x)=(1+x)^2R(x),\qquad Q(x)=(1-x)^2R(x),$$
which are nonnegative for all real $x$ (square times $R\ge0$). Since
$$(1-x)(1+x)^2+(1+x)(1-x)^2=(1-x)(1+x)\big[(1+x)+(1-x)\big]=2(1-x^2),$$
we get $(1-x)P+(1+x)Q=2(1-x^2)R=1-x^n$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $\angle BAD\le\angle ADC$. Prove that $AC+CD\le AB+BD$.
answer: Scale the circumcircle to diameter $1$: chords are sines of inscribed angles; with $x\le y$ the claim is $\sin(x+z)+\sin x\le\sin y+\sin(y+z)$, which follows from sum-to-product.

solutions.title: Law of sines and sum-to-product
solutions.body:
Let $w=\angle BAC=\angle BDC$, $x=\angle CAD=\angle CBD$, $y=\angle ACB=\angle ADB$, $z=\angle ABD=\angle ACD$ (equal inscribed angles). Then $\angle BAD=w+x$ and $\angle ADC=\angle ADB+\angle BDC=y+w$, so the hypothesis $\angle BAD\le\angle ADC$ gives $x\le y$. In triangle $ABD$, $(w+x)+y+z=180^\circ$, hence $x+y+z\le180^\circ$.

Scale so that the circumdiameter is $1$; by the extended law of sines each chord equals the sine of an inscribed angle subtending it:
$$AC=\sin\angle ABC=\sin(x+z),\quad CD=\sin x,\quad AB=\sin y,\quad BD=\sin\angle BAD=\sin(w+x)=\sin(y+z).$$
Using $\sin\alpha+\sin\beta=2\sin\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}2$,
$$AC+CD=2\sin\frac{x+z}2\cos\frac z2,\qquad AB+BD=2\sin\frac{y+z}2\cos\frac z2.$$
Now $\cos\frac z2\ge0$ since $0<z<180^\circ$. And
$$0\le\frac{x+z}2\le\frac{y+z}2\le180^\circ-\frac{x+z}2,$$
where the last inequality is $x+y+2z\le360^\circ$, true as $x+y+z\le180^\circ$ and $z\le180^\circ$. On $[a,180^\circ-a]$ the sine is at least $\sin a$, so $\sin\frac{x+z}2\le\sin\frac{y+z}2$. Therefore $AC+CD\le AB+BD$. ∎

prompt: A *lattice point* is a point in the plane whose two coordinates are both integers. A *lattice line* is a line in the plane that contains at least two lattice points. Is it possible to color every lattice point red or blue such that every lattice line contains exactly $2017$ red lattice points? Prove that your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Transfinite-free recursive construction
solutions.body:
**Answer: yes.**

A line through two lattice points contains infinitely many lattice points (all $P+k(Q-P)$, $k\in\mathbb Z$). There are countably many lattice points, hence countably many pairs of them, hence countably many lattice lines; enumerate them $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\dots$.

Start with all points blue. At step $t=1,2,\dots$ recolor finitely many blue points red, maintaining the invariant

> just before step $t$: each of $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{t-1}$ has exactly $2017$ red points, and every other line has at most $2017$.

The invariant holds before step $1$ (no red points).

**Step $t$.** Only finitely many points are red, so only finitely many lines contain two red points, so the set $S$ of lines other than $\ell_t$ having exactly $2017$ red points is finite. Each line of $S$ meets $\ell_t$ in at most one point, so the set $P$ of lattice points of $\ell_t$ lying on some line in $S$ is finite. By the invariant $\ell_t$ has at most $2017$ red points, and it has infinitely many lattice points, so we can choose blue lattice points on $\ell_t$ outside $P$ and recolor exactly as many of them red as needed to give $\ell_t$ exactly $2017$ red points.

**The invariant persists.** All new red points lie on $\ell_t$. Any line $M\ne\ell_t$ meets $\ell_t$ in at most one point, so it gains at most one red point: lines with at most $2016$ red points end with at most $2017$. Lines in $S$ (exactly $2017$) gain nothing since the new points avoid $P$; in particular $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{t-1}$ still have exactly $2017$. And $\ell_t$ now has exactly $2017$.

**The limit.** Colour a point red if it was recoloured at some step. After step $t$ the line $\ell_t$ has exactly $2017$ red points and, by the invariant, never gains another at any later step. Hence in the final colouring every lattice line $\ell_t$ has exactly $2017$ red points. ∎
